books.title: This Is a Bird
books.art_why: All the birds shown are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: This is a bird. All birds have feathers, and all birds have beaks. But all birds are different, too.
pages.brief: A single bird stands in clear view, its feathers smooth along its body and its hard beak pointing forward. Its plumage and beak are both easy to see, showing the two things every bird shares, while the bird itself looks like one particular kind of bird.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and sharp, and its feathers are black and white. It is an emperor penguin.
pages.brief: An emperor penguin stands on cold, open ground, its black and white feathers neat across its body. Its long, sharp beak points forward. The penguin holds itself upright, the black feathers on its back and the white on its front clearly divided.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and hooked, and its feathers are white. It is a pelican.
pages.brief: A pelican stands beside calm water, its white feathers bright in the open light. Its long beak is hooked at the tip, and the pelican holds its head steady, the great beak held forward above the water and the pale body resting behind it.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is sharp and hooked, and its feathers are black. It is a turkey vulture.
pages.brief: A turkey vulture stands on open ground, its black feathers dark across its body. Its sharp, hooked beak is held forward as the bird turns its bare head. The vulture stays still, the dark plumage covering its back and wings.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is short and sharp, and its feathers are white. It is a chicken.
pages.brief: A chicken stands in a farmyard setting, its white feathers clean and bright. Its short, sharp beak points forward as the chicken looks ahead. The bird stands squarely on its feet, the white plumage full across its body and neck.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and flat, and its feathers are brown. It is a mallard duck.
pages.brief: A mallard duck rests on the water, its brown feathers patterned across its body. Its long, flat beak is held low, close to the surface. The duck floats calmly, the brown plumage covering its back and sides as it faces forward.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and curved, and its feathers are brown. It is a thrasher.
pages.brief: A thrasher stands among low branches, its brown feathers blending with the twigs around it. Its long, curved beak reaches forward. The bird holds itself level, tail low, the brown plumage on its back and wings catching the light.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is short and sharp, and its feathers are red. It is a cardinal.
pages.brief: A cardinal perches on a thin branch, its red feathers vivid against the open background. Its short, sharp beak points forward. The bird sits upright and still, the bright red plumage covering its body from head to tail.

pages.text: This is a bird. Its beak is long and thin, and its feathers are purple, green, and gray. It is a Costa’s hummingbird.
pages.brief: A Costa's hummingbird hovers beside a stem, its purple, green, and gray feathers catching the light. Its long, thin beak reaches toward the blossom. The tiny bird holds itself in the air, wings a blur, the colored plumage bright on its head and body.

pages.text: In some ways, all birds are the same. All birds have beaks, and all birds have feathers. But all birds are different, too.
pages.brief: Several different birds are shown together in one open view, each with its own beak and feathers. Some beaks are long, some short, some hooked, some flat. The birds stand and perch side by side, alike in having beaks and feathers, different in every other way.

books.title: What in the World Is That?
books.art_why: The platypus is a real animal that can be photographed today.

pages.text: At the end of this book is a very strange animal. Can you guess what it is?
pages.brief: A very strange animal is the subject of a guessing question, with its identity still hidden from view. The picture sets up the mystery and asks the reader to guess what the animal could be.

pages.text: It has webbed feet to help it swim. It has a short claw on each toe. Is it a penguin?
pages.brief: A close view of webbed feet with a short claw on each toe, moving through water to show swimming. The feet are the main subject, and the page asks whether they belong to a penguin.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t have a white belly. If it’s not a penguin, what is it?
pages.brief: A close view of a belly that is not white, shown alone to rule out a penguin. The belly is the only clue in the picture, and it does not match a penguin’s white front. The animal’s other features are not revealed, leaving the guessing question open.

pages.text: Its long, flat tail helps it move through water. It lives in rivers, lakes, and ponds. Is it a beaver?
pages.brief: A long, flat tail sweeps through water in a river, lake, or pond setting, showing how it helps the animal move. The tail is the focus, and the page asks whether it belongs to a beaver.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t gnaw on trees. If it’s not a beaver, what is it?
pages.brief: A tree stands whole with no gnawing on it, ruling out a beaver. No chewed wood or tree damage is shown; the tree remains untouched. The scene leaves the question of the animal’s identity open.

pages.text: It lays small, round eggs. It has a wide bill for getting food. Is it a duck?
pages.brief: A wide bill is shown getting food, and small, round eggs lie together in the scene. The wide bill and the small, round eggs are the clues in view, and the page asks whether they belong to a duck.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t quack or have feathers. If it’s not a duck, what is it?
pages.brief: A featherless body is shown quietly, with no duck-like quacking in the scene. No feathers are visible on the animal, and no quacking sound is shown. The picture rules out a duck and keeps the mystery going.

pages.text: It has thick, shiny fur. Its long, sleek body helps it swim fast. Is it an otter?
pages.brief: A long, sleek body covered in thick, shiny fur swims fast through water. The long, sleek body and thick, shiny fur are the main clues in view, and the page asks whether the animal is an otter.

pages.text: No. It doesn’t have whiskers. If it’s not an otter, what is it?
pages.brief: A close view shows an animal with no whiskers, ruling out an otter. Only the whisker-free area is clear in the picture. The animal’s body and other features are kept out of focus so the guessing question stays open.

pages.text: It’s a platypus! What in the world is that?
pages.brief: The strange animal is revealed at last to be a platypus, shown clearly as the answer to the guessing question. Its full body is in view, and the page asks, 'What in the world is that?'

books.title: Stars and Stripes
books.art_why: The book tells the flag's history back to the thirteen colonies, long before cameras could record those days.

pages.text: Our flag has a story. The thirteen colonies that formed our country all had different flags.
pages.brief: A wide view of thirteen small colonial towns along a green coastline, each with wooden houses, a steeple and a tall pole flying its own flag. Every flag is different from the others, so they can be compared at a glance, under a wide open sky.

pages.text: We needed one flag for all of the United States. We made a flag that had thirteen bright stars and thirteen bold stripes.
pages.brief: One large new flag spread flat on a wooden table, thirteen bright white stars in a ring in the blue corner and thirteen bold stripes running its length. Beside it the old colony flags lie folded and set aside, so the single new flag stands out clearly.

pages.text: We made our new flag in red, white, and blue. We called our flag the Stars and Stripes.
pages.brief: The finished flag in red, white and blue lifted on a wooden pole against a bright sky, its thirteen stars and thirteen stripes crisp and clear. Deep blue behind the stars, deep red stripes, clean white between them, the cloth lifting in the breeze.

pages.text: Our country grew so we added two new stars and two new stripes. A famous song was written about this flag.
pages.brief: The flag on a tall pole, now with fifteen stars and fifteen stripes instead of thirteen. Near its base an open sheet of music rests on a wooden stand, notes inked across the page, freshly written for this flag.

pages.text: ATLANTIC OCEAN GULF OF MEXICO Our country grew more and more. We needed to change our flag again.
pages.brief: A simple map of the United States spread across a table, the country's outline stretching wider and wider, sea along the east and a gulf to the south. Beside the map the old flag looks out of date, its star count no longer matching the land.

pages.text: ATLANTIC OCEAN GULF OF MEXICO We went back to having thirteen stripes on the flag. The stripes show our country began with thirteen states.
pages.brief: A close look at the flag's thirteen red and white stripes running side to side, equal and bold. Behind them a small map of thirteen states shows where the country began, so the stripes and the first states line up together.

pages.text: We added a star for each new state that joined our country. The star pattern changed as their numbers grew.
pages.brief: Four flags in a row, each with more stars than the last, every one keeping thirteen stripes. The stars sit in different patterns — rings, rows and neat blocks — as new states joined, showing how the arrangement kept changing.

pages.text: Now our flag has fifty stars for our fifty states. Will there be another star added someday?
pages.brief: The flag on a tall silver pole seen from below against a clear blue sky, fifty white stars in the blue corner and thirteen stripes. The stars are lined in even rows and the whole flag ripples and snaps in the wind.

pages.text: June 14th is Flag Day. We fly our stars and stripes on Flag Day.
pages.brief: A family on the front porch of a house on a June morning, raising a flag on a pole in the yard with hands on the rope. The red, white and blue ripples above the garden, and a second flag flies from a neighbour's roof.

pages.text: We remember the story of our flag. It is a story that hasn’t ended yet!
pages.brief: A large flag waving across the sky at sunset, its fifty stars and thirteen stripes bright and clear. Behind it faint older flags — one with thirteen stars in a ring, one with fifteen — float like earlier pages of the same story, still going on.

books.title: All Kinds of Homes
books.art_why: Real homes people live in today can be photographed.

pages.text: Where Do People Live? People live in homes. Not all homes are the same. Homes can be big or small. They can be made of different things.
pages.brief: A wide view shows several homes of different sizes standing near one another, some small and some big, built from different materials such as wood, brick and concrete. A few people stand outside their homes, going about their day.

pages.text: Houses A house is one kind of home. It stands on its own. It has its own roof and front door.
pages.brief: One house stands on its own in a neighbourhood, with its own roof above and its own front door facing the street. A path leads up to the door, and the house sits apart from the buildings around it.

pages.text: Apartments Apartments are another kind of home. They have one roof. Neighbors live on other floors.
pages.brief: A tall apartment building rises with one wide roof on top and rows of windows on every floor. Neighbours stand on different balconies and walk on the stairs, living above and below one another.

pages.text: Cabins A cabin is another kind of home. It has trees and birds as neighbors. It can be made of logs.
pages.brief: A cabin made of stacked logs sits among tall trees. Birds perch on branches and hop on the ground nearby, and the wooden walls show the round ends of the logs. Trees surround it on every side.

pages.text: Motor Homes A motor home is another kind of home. It has wheels. It can move from place to place.
pages.brief: A motor home with wheels stands on a road, its body shaped like a small house. It is parked in one spot now, with the open road stretching ahead, ready to carry it on to another place.

pages.text: Houseboats A houseboat is another kind of home. It floats on water. It has fish and other boats as neighbors.
pages.brief: A houseboat floats on calm water, shaped like a small house with windows and a roof. Fish swim beneath the surface and other boats bob nearby, sharing the water with it as neighbours.

pages.text: Special Homes These homes are not like any others. They may be in a unique place. They may not look like homes you have seen.
pages.brief: A home unlike the others stands in an unusual setting, its shape different from any house, apartment, cabin, motor home or houseboat seen before. The ground around it and the view behind look unlike an ordinary street.

pages.text: Conclusion Homes can be the same in some ways. Homes can also be different in many ways.
pages.brief: Several homes from the book appear side by side: a house, an apartment building, a log cabin, a motor home and a houseboat. They all give shelter, yet each one looks different in size, shape and material.

pages.text: Some homes are very different. Which home would you like to live in?
pages.brief: A cluster of very different homes is shown, each one strange and unlike the rest. The view opens out toward the reader, as if asking which of these unusual homes someone would choose to live in.

books.title: Caring for Your Dog
books.art_why: The book shows real dogs and family care in everyday settings.

pages.text: A dog is part of your family. Adding a new dog to your family takes time and special care.
pages.brief: A dog sits close with a family in a cozy home, shown as part of the family. Family members spend time together caring for the new dog with gentle attention and patience, showing that adding a dog takes time and special care.

pages.text: Choosing a new dog is lots of fun. Choose a dog that fits in with your family.
pages.brief: A family looks at a friendly dog together, choosing a new dog that fits with their family. The dog is calm and happy with them in a simple home setting, and the family's faces show that choosing a dog is lots of fun.

pages.text: Does your family spend lots of active time outdoors? Does your family stay at home or like to travel?
pages.brief: A family and a dog are shown outdoors being active together and at home together. The scene suggests a family thinking about whether they like to travel, stay home, or spend lots of active time outdoors with a dog.

pages.text: Your family should know all of the things your dog needs. Every dog needs a place to run and play.
pages.brief: A family stands with their dog in a safe outdoor space where the dog can run and play. Family members watch and learn what the dog needs, showing that a family should know all the things their dog needs every day.

pages.text: Your dog needs to be fed twice a day. Your dog needs water all day long.
pages.brief: A dog eats from a bowl while a family member sets down food, and a water bowl stays nearby. The scene shows the dog being fed twice a day and having water available all day long.

pages.text: Walking is important for your dog’s health. Your dog needs to be walked twice a day.
pages.brief: A family member walks a dog on a leash outdoors. The dog moves along beside the person, showing that walking is important for the dog's health and that the dog needs to be walked twice a day.

pages.text: Your dog needs to be played with. You can give your dog treats if he or she is good.
pages.brief: A child plays with a happy dog, and the dog looks good and calm. The child offers a treat to the dog because it is good, showing that a dog needs to be played with and can get treats for good behavior.

pages.text: Your dog needs to be brushed and washed.
pages.brief: A family member brushes a dog's coat, and nearby the dog is being washed with gentle care. The dog stays calm as it gets brushed and washed, showing the care it needs to stay clean at home.

pages.text: Your dog needs a warm place to sleep.
pages.brief: A dog curls up in a warm, comfortable sleeping place indoors, with soft bedding around it. The dog rests with its eyes closed and looks peaceful, showing that it needs a warm place to sleep.

pages.text: Most of all, your dog needs a family and lots of love!
pages.brief: A dog sits close with a loving family in their home, surrounded by gentle affection. Family members pet and hug the dog with warm smiles, showing that most of all the dog needs a family and lots of love.

books.title: The Spider's Web
books.art_why: A spider, a web and a fly are real things that can be photographed today.

pages.text: The spider needs to build a new web. The web will help her catch her food.
pages.brief: One small spider stands alone on a green leafy plant, her eight legs resting on the leaf. She has no web around her yet as she gets ready to make something new: a web that will help her catch her food.

pages.text: She chooses a branch to start on. She spins out a thread of sticky silk.
pages.brief: The spider walks along a thin brown branch. She lifts her body and pulls a long, shiny thread of sticky silk out from her body, letting the silk trail behind her along the wood.

pages.text: She sticks the silk to the branch below. She sticks more silk threads between the two branches.
pages.brief: The spider fastens the first silk thread to a lower branch, pressing it down so it sticks. Then she stretches more sticky threads across the gap, until several thin lines connect the upper branch and the lower branch.

pages.text: She crawls around and around, spinning silk. She makes many circles to make the web strong.
pages.brief: The spider crawls around and around between the branches, spinning silk as she goes. She traces many circles, crossing the straight threads again and again, until the round web looks strong and full.

pages.text: Soon, her web is done. The spider waits quietly.
pages.brief: The web is finished, a round silvery circle stretched between the branches. The spider sits still at the edge of her web and waits quietly, her legs touching the silk, watching for something to come.

pages.text: A fly gets stuck in the threads of the web.
pages.brief: A fly drops into the web and its legs catch in the sticky threads. The fly's wings buzz and it struggles, held fast by the silk, while the spider's web shakes where the fly is stuck.

pages.text: The spider creeps toward the fly.
pages.brief: The spider creeps slowly along the silk toward the struggling fly. Her legs grip the threads as she steps closer, keeping her body low over the web, moving in on the trapped insect.

pages.text: The spider bites the fly.
pages.brief: Close beside the fly, the spider bites it, pressing her mouth parts into the small insect caught in the web. The fly's wings stop buzzing and it goes still in the sticky silk.

pages.text: She wraps the fly in silk.
pages.brief: The spider wraps the fly in silk. She turns the fly over and over, pulling fresh thread from her body and winding it around the insect until the fly is covered in a tight, pale bundle of silk.

pages.text: The spider’s bite changes the fly’s body into goo. When the spider is hungry, she drinks the goo!
pages.brief: The spider bites the wrapped fly again, and her bite turns the fly's body inside the silk into soft goo. Later, when she is hungry, the spider drinks the goo from the bundle.

books.title: American Symbols
books.art_why: All the symbols shown are real things that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Many Symbols The United States has many symbols. A symbol is something that stands for something else. Symbols can be different things.
pages.brief: A wide, clear scene introducing the idea of symbols: a group of different symbol objects, each one a different shape and size, sits together with open space around them so each can be seen separately and compared.

pages.text: American Flag The U.S. flag is an American symbol. It is red, white, and blue.
pages.brief: A large American flag fills the frame, waving in the open air, its red, white and blue stripes and blue star field clearly visible as it ripples in the breeze against a plain sky.

pages.text: The flag has fifty stars. Each star stands for one of the fifty states.
pages.brief: A close, sharp view of the blue corner of the American flag, where row upon row of white stars are sewn, each star standing out clearly against the deep blue cloth.

pages.text: Bald Eagle The bald eagle is an American symbol. It is strong and beautiful.
pages.brief: A bald eagle with a white head and dark brown body, strong yellow beak and bright eyes, perched upright on a thick branch, its feathers sharp and clean in bright daylight.

pages.text: The bald eagle stands for how strong and beautiful the United States is. You can see the bald eagle on some coins.
pages.brief: A bald eagle on a branch beside a few United States coins spread out on a plain surface, the eagle's shape stamped clearly on the metal of each coin.

pages.text: Statue of Liberty The Statue of Liberty is an American symbol. It is on an island near New York City.
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty stands tall on its island in the harbour, green copper figure holding its torch high, with the buildings of New York City visible across the water in the distance.

pages.text: The statue has welcomed many people to the United States. It stands for freedom and hope for a better life. The statue was a gift of friendship from France.
pages.brief: The Statue of Liberty rises above a group of people arriving at the island, looking up at the statue with their bags and belongings, the harbour water and city behind them.

pages.text: Important Ideas The United States has many different symbols. They stand for ideas that are important to people in the United States.
pages.brief: The three American symbols from the book shown together in one scene: the flag flying, the bald eagle perched nearby, and the Statue of Liberty standing on its island, grouped to show many symbols in one country.

pages.text: What other U.S. symbols can you think of?
pages.brief: A calm, open scene with the flag, the bald eagle and the Statue of Liberty placed together with wide empty space around them, as if waiting for more symbols to be added to the group.

books.title: Why Do Leaves Change Color?
books.art_why: Real trees and leaves can be photographed.

pages.text: So Many Colors Why are leaves on trees different colors? What makes them change color?
pages.brief: A view of several trees outdoors, each with leaves in different colors. The leaves on the trees are not all the same color. The trees stand together in a natural setting with many leaves on their branches.

pages.text: Making Food Leaves make food for the tree from sunlight, water, and air. Green stuff in the leaves helps them make food. It also makes the leaves green.
pages.brief: Green leaves on a tree branch spread out in bright sunlight, with water droplets on their surfaces and open air around them. The green color in the leaves helps the tree make food from sunlight, water, and air.

pages.text: Summer Leaves are green because they are making food. The tree saves some food for winter.
pages.brief: A big tree covered in green leaves stands in warm summer sunshine. Its branches are full of green leaves. The tree is making food in the summer light and saves some food for winter.

pages.text: Fall In fall, the weather changes. The days get shorter. The nights get longer. Trees get less sunlight, so they make less food.
pages.brief: A tree outdoors in fall under a lower, dimmer sky, with the light fading around it. The weather changes as fall comes. The days are shorter and the nights are longer, so the tree gets less sunlight.

pages.text: The leaves stop making the green color. Other colors that were under the green start to show.
pages.brief: A close-up of leaves on a branch, with green fading and yellow and orange colors beginning to show through. The leaves have stopped making the green color, so other colors that were under the green start to show.

pages.text: Leaves turn yellow, orange, brown, and red.
pages.brief: Leaves on a tree have turned yellow, orange, brown, and red. Some leaves are yellow, some orange, some brown, and some red. The different colored leaves are spread across the branches in fall, showing several colors together.

pages.text: Winter Trees drop their leaves to get ready for winter. They use the food they saved to get through the cold days and nights.
pages.brief: A bare tree stands in cold winter weather, with no leaves on its branches. The tree has dropped its leaves to get ready for winter and is using saved food to get through the cold days and nights.

pages.text: Spring Spring comes. Ice and snow melt, and rain falls. The Sun shines. New leaves grow on the trees.
pages.brief: A tree stands outdoors in spring as ice and snow melt and rain falls from the sky. The Sun shines, and small new leaves begin to grow on the branches of the tree, bringing new growth.

pages.text: The green leaves start making food again.
pages.brief: Green leaves on a tree branch in bright spring sunlight. The leaves are green again and have started making food for the tree from sunlight, water, and air. The green color has returned to the leaves.

books.title: Wiggly Worms
books.art_why: Earthworms, soil and gardens are real today, so real photographs work.

pages.text: orms Wiggly Worms.
pages.brief: Several pink earthworms wriggle through dark, damp garden soil, their long ringed bodies bent and curling in different directions. Crumbs of soil and small pebbles surround them as they stretch and pull themselves through the earth, twisting and turning.

pages.text: orms iggly orms.
pages.brief: A close view of wiggly earthworms moving through soft brown soil. Two or three worms curve and loop over one another, their bodies bending as they travel. Damp earth and tiny stones press around them, and the worms keep squirming through the dark ground.

pages.text: Small Animals, Big Changes Do you know about earthworms? These small animals change the soil in big ways.
pages.brief: Earthworms tunnel through garden soil beneath green plants. One worm pushes through a clump of earth, breaking it into smaller crumbs, while others move nearby. Above the soil, small plants stand in a garden bed, showing how these small animals change the ground.

pages.text: Earthworm Bodies The body of an earthworm is made up of many parts. Each part is shaped like a ring. Each part can bend and stretch. Earthworms move by stretching and pulling their bodies. saddle mouth head end before stretching out to move after stretching out to move tail end rings.
pages.brief: An earthworm shown close up, its body made of many ring-shaped parts that bend and stretch. One view shows the worm bunched up short before stretching, another shows it pulled out long to move. Its mouth and head end are at the front, the saddle and tail end behind, resting on damp soil.

pages.text: Slimy Worms! Earthworms are slimy. The slime helps keep earthworms cool and wet. It also helps earthworms slide through soil. After worms mate, a ball of slime forms. The slime dries into a cocoon. Baby worms come out of the cocoon.
pages.brief: A worm covered in shiny slime rests on a log, leaving a wet slime trail behind it. Nearby, a ball of slime has dried into a small cocoon, and baby worms come out of it. Damp wood and soil show where the slime helps the worm slide along.

pages.text: Earthworm Behavior Earthworms build long tunnels underground. The tunnels keep worms away from heat and sunlight. They also help earthworms hide from hungry animals.
pages.brief: Under the ground, earthworms have built long tunnels through the soil. A worm moves along a tunnel far below the surface, away from hot sunlight, while other worms travel through branching tunnels. The deep, dark passages keep them hidden from animals that would eat them.

pages.text: Earthworms come out at night to look for food. Some people call them night crawlers. Earthworms eat dead leaves and plants.
pages.brief: At night, earthworms come out of the soil onto the surface, looking for food. One worm stretches toward a dead leaf, another toward a fallen plant stem on the dark ground. Damp earth and night shadows show the worms crawling out to feed on dead leaves and plants.

pages.text: Earthworms Are Good for the Soil Farmers love earthworms! Earthworms make space in the soil. The space helps plants get what they need to grow. Earthworm waste helps plants grow big and strong.
pages.brief: A farmer stands in a garden bed, smiling at earthworms in the soil. The worms have made spaces between crumbs of earth, and a nearby plant stands tall with strong green leaves, showing how the spaces and earthworm waste help plants grow big and strong.

pages.text: Wanted: Earthworms! Many animals love to eat earthworms.
pages.brief: Earthworms lie in damp soil while animals nearby search for them to eat. Worms twist through the earth as hungry animals hunt around the garden ground, showing that many animals love to eat earthworms. Loose soil and plants fill the scene.

pages.text: Earthworms are small, but they have a big job. Earthworms help plants grow!
pages.brief: Small earthworms move through the soil beneath a healthy green plant, with tunnels and spaces around them. The plant above stands tall with wide leaves, showing the big job these tiny worms do as they help plants grow.

books.title: Ride, Cling, Run
books.art_why: All the animals shown are real living species that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Animals Come and Go Many animals travel from place to place. They travel to find food, water, and shelter.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor scene showing several kinds of animals on the move across open ground and near water: a lion family walking, birds overhead, a fish in a stream. The animals are travelling away from dry ground toward food, water and shelter, spread out across the landscape.

pages.text: Baby animals often travel with their parents. They may ride, cling, or run with their parents.
pages.brief: A parent animal with its baby close beside it in a natural setting. The baby is held in the parent's mouth, gripping the parent's back, and trotting along behind, showing three different ways young animals stay with their mothers and fathers as they travel.

pages.text: Ride Baby lions are called cubs. Some cubs ride in their mother’s mouth. Lions sleep in dens.
pages.brief: A lion mother in a shady den with her small cubs. One cub is carried gently in her mouth while the others lie close by on the ground. The den is a sheltered spot among rocks and dry grass where the lion family rests and sleeps.

pages.text: Baby fish hatch from eggs. Some baby fish ride in their father’s mouth. Fish live in water.
pages.brief: Underwater view of a fish father with tiny baby fish swimming around him. Several of the smallest babies are held inside his open mouth, while other baby fish hover nearby in the clear water above smooth stones and water plants.

pages.text: Cling Baby spiders hatch from eggs. Some baby spiders cling to their mother’s back. Most spiders climb on webs.
pages.brief: A close view of a spider mother on a leafy plant with her newly hatched babies clustered on her back. The tiny spiders cling tightly to her. Nearby, another spider climbs a thin web strung between stems.

pages.text: Baby frogs hatch from eggs. Some baby frogs cling to their father’s back. Frogs can live in water and on land.
pages.brief: A small frog father sitting on damp ground at the edge of a pond, with several tiny baby frogs clinging to his back. Green plants and shallow water surround him, showing a place where frogs can live both in water and on land.

pages.text: Run Baby penguins hatch from eggs. Baby penguins run behind their parents. Penguins like to swim, but they can also run.
pages.brief: A penguin parent walking across icy ground with baby penguins running in a line behind it. Snow and blue water lie in the background, showing that these penguins can swim in the sea but also run on land.

pages.text: Baby wolves are called pups. The pups run with their parents. Wolves sleep in dens.
pages.brief: A wolf den among rocks and grass, with grey wolf pups running close behind their parents across the ground. The adult wolves lead the way while the pups follow, and the sheltered den opening is visible behind them.

pages.text: Ride, Cling, Run Baby opossums are called joeys. First, joeys ride in their mother’s pouch. Then, they cling to their mother’s back. Later, they run from place to place.
pages.brief: An opossum mother in a tree with her joeys at three stages: one tiny joey inside her pouch, one gripping the fur on her back, and older joeys moving along a branch away from her, travelling from place to place through the woodland.

books.title: Are You From Australia?
books.art_why: Real Australian animals and places exist today, so photographs suit the book.

pages.text: I live in Australia. It is a large country with lots of open space. Many animals live here.
pages.brief: A child stands in a large, open Australian landscape with wide grassy space and scattered trees, looking out over the country. Many animals live here; several of them appear in the distance across the open ground, showing that this is a country with lots of space.

pages.text: I live in the rivers of Australia. I look like a beaver with a duck’s bill. I eat tasty bugs on the river bottom.
pages.brief: A platypus swims along the bottom of a river in Australia. It has a flat, beaver-like tail and a duck’s bill. It noses through the riverbed, eating tasty bugs. Its bill and tail are clearly visible.

pages.text: I live in the forests of Australia. I am one of the biggest bats in the world. I eat sweet fruit and flowers.
pages.brief: A large bat flies through a forest in Australia. It is one of the biggest bats in the world. It eats sweet fruit and flowers, and fruit and blossoms are nearby in the trees. The bat feeds among the branches.

pages.text: I live in the deserts of Australia. I hop on two big legs. I carry my baby in a pouch.
pages.brief: A kangaroo stands in a desert in Australia, hopping on two big legs. It carries its baby in a pouch on its front. The baby is inside the pouch. The desert ground is dry and open.

pages.text: I live in the deserts and forests of Australia. I roll into a ball when I am scared. I eat yummy ants.
pages.brief: An animal stands in a desert or forest in Australia. When scared, it rolls into a ball. It eats yummy ants, with its snout near an ant trail on the ground. Its body is curled tight.

pages.text: I live in the trees of Australia. I make my nest with leaves. I am yellow with a green body.
pages.brief: A yellow bird with a green body sits in a tree in Australia. It makes a nest with leaves. The nest is among the branches, and the bird is near it. The bird works on the leafy nest.

pages.text: I live on the seashore of Australia. I dig holes in the sand to lay eggs. I catch fish in the sea.
pages.brief: A sea turtle is on the seashore in Australia. It digs a hole in the sand to lay eggs. The sand is beside the water. Later, the turtle is in the sea, catching fish. The turtle moves between shore and sea.

pages.text: I live in the trees of Australia. I eat nothing but special leaves.
pages.brief: A koala sits in a tree in Australia. It eats nothing but special leaves. The leaves are around it on the branches, and the koala holds a leafy branch. The tree is full of leaves.

pages.text: I live in the waters of Australia. I swim in rivers, lakes, and even the sea.
pages.brief: An animal swims in the waters of Australia. It moves through a river, a lake, and even the sea. The water is around it as it swims. The animal is shown swimming in each kind of water.

pages.text: All of these animals are from Australia, and I am from Australia, too!
pages.brief: A child stands with all the animals—the platypus, big bat, kangaroo, ant-eating animal, yellow-and-green bird, sea turtle, koala, and water animal—in Australia. They are all together, showing they are from Australia. The child is from Australia too.

books.title: A Taste for Blood
books.art_why: All the blood-drinking animals shown are real creatures that can be photographed today.

pages.text: All animals need to eat food to live. For some animals, that food is another animal’s blood.
pages.brief: A close, natural view of several different animals feeding: a small bird holding a berry in its beak, a rabbit nibbling grass, a butterfly on a flower. In the corner of the same scene, a tiny insect rests on the skin of a larger animal, taking its food from it.

pages.text: Female mosquitoes drink blood. These small insects leave marks that itch.
pages.brief: A female mosquito stands on bare human skin, thin legs spread, its needle-like mouth pushed into the skin. The skin around the bite is already raised in a small red itchy lump. Soft green leaves blur in the background behind the arm.

pages.text: Some lampreys drink blood. These fish have round mouths full of little teeth.
pages.brief: An underwater view of a lamprey attached to the side of a fish, its round mouth pressed against the flesh. The circular mouth is open and packed with rows of small sharp teeth. Murky river water and smooth stones fill the background.

pages.text: Some bats drink blood. These mammals fly out to feed at night.
pages.brief: A blood-drinking bat hangs or flutters in deep blue night, wings spread, small face forward. Others of its kind lift away from a dark cave mouth or tree roost behind it, heading out over the night landscape to feed.

pages.text: Ticks drink blood. These animals are like spiders. They hide on leaves or grass. They grab onto animals that walk past them.
pages.brief: A tick clings to the tip of a green grass blade, its small flat body close to the leaf. Another tick waits on a low leaf nearby. Below them, the legs of an animal walking past brush through the grass, ready to be grabbed.

pages.text: Most leeches drink blood. These worms live in marshes, rivers, and ponds.
pages.brief: Leeches rest in shallow water among marsh reeds, their soft dark worm bodies stretched and curling. One is half-hidden in mud at the pond edge, another drifts in the still water. Green stems and quiet ripples surround them.

pages.text: One kind of bird drinks blood. These small birds peck at larger birds.
pages.brief: A small blood-drinking bird perches on the back of a much larger bird, head lowered as it pecks at the bigger bird's feathers and skin. The large bird stands in an open grassy place, wings folded, while the small bird works along its back.

pages.text: Bedbugs drink blood. These insects hide in and around beds.
pages.brief: Several bedbugs cluster in the dark seam of a mattress and along the wooden frame of a bed, flat oval bodies pressed into the crack. White bedding and a pillow sit above them, with more bugs hidden in the folds near the head of the bed.

pages.text: Fleas drink blood. These insects can’t fly, but they can jump very far.
pages.brief: A flea is caught mid-jump above a floor, its hard little body arched, long back legs pushing off. A second flea lands on the fur of an animal nearby. Neither has wings, yet both spring high across the room.

pages.text: Animals that drink blood have been around for a long time. You don’t want to be their next meal!
pages.brief: A group of blood-drinking animals together: a mosquito in the air, a tick on a stem, a leech in water, a bat overhead and a flea on fur. A person steps back, hands raised, away from the small crowd of feeders.

books.title: Living Or Nonliving?
books.art_why: The book shows a real brown bear, a toy robot, gears and a battery, all things that can be photographed.

pages.text: Introduction How can you tell when one thing is living and another is not? This brown bear is a living thing. This toy robot is not.
pages.brief: A brown bear is shown as a living thing, and a simple toy robot is shown as nonliving. They appear side by side so viewers can clearly compare a real animal with a made object.

pages.text: Living and Nonliving Things Living things are alike in important ways. Living things all grow and make more things like themselves. They also use energy, move, change, and are made of cells. Nonliving things may be like living things in some ways. They may move, change, or use energy. They are not alike in all the ways, or they would be living things.
pages.brief: Living things are shown growing and making more things like themselves. They also move, change, and use energy, and cells are shown inside them. A nonliving thing is shown beside them, also moving or using energy.

pages.text: Compare Living and Nonliving Things Some of the ways they are different are easy to spot. The toy robot does not grow. It cannot make more things like itself.
pages.brief: A toy robot is shown standing in place. It stays the same size and does not grow. It cannot make more things like itself. The scene makes clear that these are easy differences between the toy robot and living things.

pages.text: Some of the ways they are alike can make it tricky. The toy robot does move and use energy. It has gears and a battery that help it move.
pages.brief: A toy robot is shown moving. Its gears turn inside it and a battery gives it energy. The robot shows a nonliving thing that moves and uses energy, which can make telling living from nonliving tricky.

pages.text: Dead Things Nonliving things are not dead. Dead things were once alive but now are not. Nonliving things were never alive. Conclusion Figuring out if something is living or nonliving can be fun. Which of these things are living or nonliving?
pages.brief: A dead thing is shown as something that was once alive but is not now. A nonliving thing is shown as something that was never alive. Viewers are invited to decide which things are living or nonliving.

books.title: Taking the Train
books.art_why: Trains, stations and city streets are real places that cameras can photograph today.

pages.text: The horn blows. The train rolls along the track.
pages.brief: A train rolls along a track, its horn blowing. The locomotive leads the cars along the rails as the train moves forward. The scene shows the train in motion, with the track stretching ahead and behind it.

pages.text: When the train stops, some people get on. Other people get off.
pages.brief: At a train stop, the train has come to a halt. Some people step onto the train through the open doors, while other people step off onto the platform. The passengers move in both directions at once.

pages.text: The train rolls along the track again. It heads toward the big city.
pages.brief: The train rolls along the track again, moving forward. In the distance, the big city rises ahead as the train heads toward it. The train and its cars travel along the rails toward the skyline.

pages.text: It goes faster as it moves along. Sometimes it races forward. Sometimes it rocks side to side.
pages.brief: The train moves faster along the track. It races forward, and sometimes it rocks side to side as it goes. The train and its cars are shown in motion, tilting slightly as they speed along the rails.

pages.text: Some people read on the train, while others rest. Some people talk to each other, while others talk on their phones.
pages.brief: Inside a train car, some people sit reading, while others rest in their seats. Some people talk to each other face to face, and others talk on their phones. The passengers fill the seats along the car.

pages.text: The train passes grassy fields. It crosses rivers. It passes stores, schools, and backyards.
pages.brief: The train passes grassy fields and crosses a river. Along the way it goes by stores, schools, and backyards. The train travels past fields and buildings, with the view changing from open country to town scenes.

pages.text: The train enters a long tunnel.
pages.brief: The train enters a long tunnel. The front of the train disappears into the dark opening, and the cars follow one by one. The tunnel stretches ahead as the train moves inside, leaving the daylight behind.

pages.text: The train arrives in the city! Here, tall buildings rise toward the sky.
pages.brief: The train arrives in the city. Tall buildings rise toward the sky all around. The train comes in among the tall buildings, and the city towers above the tracks as the train reaches its stop.

pages.text: The train makes one last stop. All the people get off. Other people get on.
pages.brief: The train makes one last stop. All the people get off the train, stepping out onto the platform. Other people get on, stepping aboard. The passengers trade places at the final stop.

pages.text: Soon the train rolls along the track again. It rolls back through the tunnel. It rolls back past towns and grassy fields. The horn blows.
pages.brief: Soon the train rolls along the track again. It rolls back through the tunnel, and back past towns and grassy fields. The horn blows as the train travels on, heading back the way it came.

books.title: Zoo Data
books.art_why: Real children, zoo animals, and enclosures can be shown in photographs.

pages.text: Allie, Jo, and Chris are going to the zoo. They will record what they see. “I’ll make a table,” says Allie. “I’ll use tallies,” says Jo. “I’ll draw a graph,” says Chris.
pages.brief: Allie, Jo, and Chris stand together at the zoo, ready to record what they see. Allie plans a table, Jo plans to use tallies, and Chris plans to draw a graph. The three friends look ahead toward the animal areas they will visit.

pages.text: First, the kids see three elephants. Allie starts her table. Animal How Many Animal Table.
pages.brief: Allie, Jo, and Chris stand near a zoo enclosure and watch three elephants. The elephants are together in their habitat. Allie begins her table, marking the elephant group, while Jo and Chris watch the elephants with her.

pages.text: Next, the kids see two bears. Jo marks her tally chart. Animal Tally Chart.
pages.brief: The three kids stop at the bear enclosure and watch two bears. Jo marks her tally chart with simple tally marks while Allie and Chris look at the bears. The bears are in their zoo habitat as the kids record the second animal group.

pages.text: Then, the kids see four wolves. Chris draws his graph. Wolf Bear Elephant Animal Graph.
pages.brief: Allie, Jo, and Chris watch four wolves in a zoo habitat. Chris draws his graph on paper, showing the wolf group, while Allie and Jo look on. The wolves stand and move together behind the enclosure as the kids record what they see.

pages.text: Animal Tally Chart Which group has the most animals? How many animals are there in all? Animal Table Animal How Many Elephant 3 Bear 2 Wolf.
pages.brief: The kids look over their tally chart and table, comparing the elephant, bear, and wolf groups. They pause to think about which group has the most animals and how many animals they counted in all. Allie, Jo, and Chris stand together at the zoo with their recording pages.

pages.text: Animal Graph Animal Table Animal How Many Elephant 3 Bear 2 Wolf 4 Did all of the kids find the same information?
pages.brief: Allie, Jo, and Chris gather their graph, table, and tally chart at the zoo. They look at the elephant, bear, and wolf counts and wonder whether all of them found the same information. The three friends stand together with their finished recording pages, ready to compare what they have.

books.title: Squirrel Acrobats
books.art_why: Gray squirrels exist today and can be photographed in the wild.

pages.text: Gray squirrels are some of nature’s acrobats. They move quickly and easily to find food or escape from other animals.
pages.brief: Gray squirrels move quickly and easily through a woodland, some on the ground and some near branches, alert as they search for food or prepare to escape from other animals. Their bodies look nimble and ready to dart away at any moment.

pages.text: They dart or dash across the ground. They can stop quickly with their tails up. They are alert for danger. They whip their tails from side to side if they see other animals.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel darts across the ground and stops quickly with its tail held up. It looks alert for danger, and when another animal appears, it whips its tail from side to side. Its eyes watch the surroundings.

pages.text: They move fast on the ground. They run and leap quickly so that cats or foxes do not catch them.
pages.brief: Gray squirrels run and leap fast across the ground, their tails streaming behind them. A cat and a fox are nearby, but the squirrels stay ahead, moving quickly so the animals do not catch them.

pages.text: They cling to tree trunks with their claws.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel clings to a rough tree trunk with its small claws. Its body is pressed close to the bark, and it holds on tightly while looking around the woodland from its place on the tree.

pages.text: They can climb and change direction quickly. They can change direction to escape from birds or other squirrels.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel climbs a tree trunk and changes direction quickly, twisting to one side. Nearby, a bird and another squirrel are visible as the first squirrel turns away to escape them. Its feet grip the bark.

pages.text: They can leap easily from large branches to small ones.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel leaps from a large branch toward a much smaller branch. Its body stretches through the air, legs spread and tail extended, as it makes the easy jump between branches high in the tree.

pages.text: They land easily on small branches by using their tails. They use their tails to keep their balance and not fall off.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel lands on a small branch, using its tail to keep its balance so it does not fall off. Its tail is spread out behind it, helping it stay steady on the narrow branch.

pages.text: Small branches or wires are like tightropes that they easily run across.
pages.brief: A gray squirrel runs easily across a small branch, and another runs along a thin wire, both like tightropes above the ground. Their bodies stay steady as they cross, and the branch and wire stretch through the air.

pages.text: They can hang from the bottoms of branches. They can even climb upside down!
pages.brief: A gray squirrel hangs from the underside of a branch, holding on with its claws. Another squirrel climbs upside down along a branch above it, showing how easily the animals can move in unusual positions.

pages.text: Squirrel acrobats can quickly and easily climb, leap, and run!
pages.brief: Gray squirrels climb, leap, and run quickly and easily through the trees. One squirrel springs between branches while others race along trunks and across branches, all moving with speed and balance in the woodland. Their tails stream behind them.

books.title: Meet the Beetles
books.art_why: Beetles are real animals living today, so real photographs are possible.

pages.text: Beetles are amazing insects. Like other insects, beetles have three main body parts.
pages.brief: A single large beetle rests on a smooth green leaf, seen very close up in bright daylight. Its body is clearly divided into three sections from head to rear, and its six legs and two antennae show against the leaf. Soft green background, sharp focus on the insect.

pages.text: Most beetles have two pairs of wings. The front wings are hard and thick to protect the pair underneath.
pages.brief: A beetle clings to a rough tree trunk with its hard, thick outer wings lifted slightly open. Beneath them a second pair of thin, see-through wings lies folded. Warm sunlight, blurred woodland behind, the insect filling most of the frame.

pages.text: All beetles have a hard skeleton on the outside of their bodies. The skeleton protects the beetles.
pages.brief: Extreme close-up of a beetle's back, showing the shiny hard outer casing that covers its whole body like armour. The surface catches the light, ridged in places, with the head and legs just visible at the edges. Plain soft background so the shell stands out.

pages.text: There are many different kinds of beetles. There are more kinds of beetles than any other living thing.
pages.brief: Many different beetles are gathered on a patch of bark and moss: a long thin one, a round spotted one, a shiny dark one and a small reddish one. They are spread out side by side, each a different shape and size, in soft natural light.

pages.text: Beetles can live almost anywhere. Beetles can live in forests. Beetles can live in deserts.
pages.brief: Two beetle habitats shown together: one beetle walking over leaf litter and moss on a shady forest floor among tall trunks, and another beetle crossing rippled desert sand under a wide empty sky. Both insects are close to the ground in warm natural light.

pages.text: Beetles can live in jungles. Beetles can even live in and around water.
pages.brief: A beetle climbs a broad wet jungle leaf, dripping with moisture, ferns and thick green plants crowding behind it. Below, a second beetle moves along the muddy edge of a shallow pool, legs on the wet stones. Humid, dappled light.

pages.text: Beetles change several times as they grow. Each time they change, they look very different.
pages.brief: Three stages of one beetle shown together along a leafy twig: a segmented grub-like young one, a still resting case, and a fully grown beetle with hard wing cases. Each looks completely different in shape and colour, arranged in a row in soft daylight.

pages.text: Beetles eat many different things. Some beetles eat dead plants and animals.
pages.brief: A beetle stands on a rotting log beside fallen brown leaves and the remains of a small dead creature, its mouthparts close to the soft decaying material. Damp dark soil and fallen twigs surround it on a shaded forest floor, the insect sharply in focus.

pages.text: Some beetles eat animal waste. Some beetles eat plants. Some beetles eat other insects.
pages.brief: Three beetles shown in a row, each doing something different: one on a pile of animal droppings in a field, one nibbling the edge of a green leaf, and one facing a small insect on a stone. Grass and soil beneath, bright daylight, all three clearly visible.

pages.text: Beetles are amazing insects!
pages.brief: A single beetle fills the frame, standing on a curved green stem against a soft, glowing background. Its hard wing cases, six legs and antennae are crisp and detailed, colours bright. The insect is seen from the side, calm and still, in warm evening light.

books.title: Scorpions
books.art_why: Scorpions, spiders and ticks are real animals that can be photographed today.

pages.text: Scorpions are arachnids. Spiders and ticks are arachnids, too. scorpion tick.
pages.brief: A scorpion with its pincers forward stands on dry sandy ground. Beside it, a spider rests on a leaf and a small tick clings to a blade of grass, all three shown close up so their body shapes can be compared.

pages.text: All arachnids have a hard shell. All arachnids have two body parts and eight legs.
pages.brief: Close view of a scorpion from above, a hard glossy shell covering two body parts, eight legs spread on the ground and a tail curving behind. A spider is shown nearby with the same two-part body and eight legs.

pages.text: Scorpions also have a pair of claws. Scorpions use their claws to grab prey.
pages.brief: A scorpion grips a small insect in its open claws, holding the prey up off the ground. Its eight legs are braced on a rock in dry country as the claws close tightly around the catch.

pages.text: Scorpions also have a long tail. At the end of the tail is a stinger. The stinger has venom in it.
pages.brief: A scorpion seen from the side, its long tail arched high over its back and ending in a sharp stinger. At the tip of the stinger a bead of venom glistens in the light.

pages.text: Scorpions use their tail to sting animals that try to hurt them. Scorpions use their tail to sting prey, too. Scorpions come out at night to hunt for prey.
pages.brief: At night, a scorpion raises its tail and drives the stinger into a small animal that has come too close. On moonlit desert sand another scorpion hunts, tail ready, searching for prey in the dark.

pages.text: Scorpions eat a lot at one time. Scorpions eat a lot of different small animals. Some scorpions eat other scorpions!
pages.brief: A scorpion feeding on a big meal of several small animals gathered together, its claws holding the food while it eats. Nearby a larger scorpion grips a smaller scorpion, showing that some scorpions eat other scorpions.

pages.text: There are about 1,500 kinds of scorpions. Some scorpions are small. Some scorpions are big.
pages.brief: Two scorpions shown for size, a tiny one beside a small stone and a big one filling the frame behind it. Both stand on dry sandy ground with claws forward and tails curled, showing how much scorpions differ in size.

pages.text: Some scorpions are blue or green. Some scorpions are yellow or red.
pages.brief: Four scorpions shown in different colours on sand and rock: one deep blue, one green, one yellow and one red, each with claws forward and tail curled, standing in daylight so their colours can be compared.

pages.text: Some scorpions glow in the dark!
pages.brief: In darkness a scorpion glows pale blue-green, its hard shell, claws, eight legs and curved tail all shining with the glow. It stands on sandy desert ground, the only bright thing in the night scene.

books.title: Signs Are Everywhere
books.art_why: Signs on posts, buildings, windows and roads exist in the real world today and can be photographed.

pages.text: Signs are everywhere. Signs are on posts. Signs are on buildings. Signs are in windows and on doors. They hang above streets. Where else do you see signs?
pages.brief: A busy street corner where signs appear in many places at once: a metal sign fixed to a post, a large sign on the side of a building, a small sign taped in a shop window and one on a glass door. A wide sign hangs above the street on a frame, and people walk past below it.

pages.text: Signs tell us lots of things. Signs tell us what to do. They tell us when to walk and when not to walk. They tell us when to stop and when to go. Signs tell us where to go and where not to go. They tell us how far to go and how fast we can go. What do these signs tell us?
pages.brief: A pedestrian crossing with a signal showing a walking figure, and further along a red stop sign and a green go signal. A one-way arrow sign points along the road, a sign shows a distance in miles, and a round sign displays a speed limit, all beside the pavement where people pass.

pages.text: Signs give us warnings. They warn us about children playing. They warn us about animals on the road. They tell us to drive slowly on winding roads. What do these signs warn us about?
pages.brief: Three roadside warning signs in a row: a yellow diamond showing children playing near a school, a sign with a deer or cow standing on the road, and a sign with a curving arrow for a winding road. Trees and a curving stretch of tarmac sit behind them.

pages.text: People make signs for lots of things. They make signs for sales. They make signs for lost animals. People make signs to advertise things. What other things do people make signs for?
pages.brief: People making and using signs: a shop worker taping a bright sale sign in a window, a printed sign on a lamp post with a picture of a missing dog and a phone number strip, and a large advertising board on a wall showing a product poster while shoppers walk by outside.

books.title: Places People Live
books.art_why: Real places and homes that exist today can be photographed.

pages.text: People live in many different places. They live where it is cold. They live where it is hot. They live where it is dry. They live where it is wet.
pages.brief: A wide outdoor scene showing several kinds of settlements: snowy cold homes in the distance, hot sunny houses, dry desert dwellings and wet rainy homes near water, each with people going about their day outside.

pages.text: Some people like to live high up. A few people live way high up. Some people live down low. Some people even live below the ground.
pages.brief: A hillside view with homes built high up on a slope, other houses down low in a valley below, and a small underground home with a doorway set into the earth, people visible near each.

pages.text: People live in many different kinds of houses. They live in houses made of stone. They live in houses made of grass. They live in houses made of sticks. They live in houses made of glass. People even live in houses made of ice.
pages.brief: A row of different real houses side by side: one of stone, one of grass thatch, one of sticks, one of glass and one of ice blocks, each standing in its own setting under open sky.

pages.text: Some people live high above the ground. Some people live deep below the water. Some people live in the ground. Some people build homes in caves or on cliffs.
pages.brief: A coastal cliff scene with homes perched high on the rock, a house under the water below, a home dug into the ground and cave openings in the cliff where people live.

pages.text: Some people live in houses that move. Some houses are on wheels. And some float on the water. Houses can be strange. They can have strange shapes. They can be made of strange things. But no matter what it is, a house is a home.
pages.brief: A moving homes scene showing a house on wheels travelling a road and a floating houseboat on calm water, with oddly shaped real houses nearby in bright daylight.

books.title: The Food We Eat
books.art_why: Foods, plants, animals and farms are real and can be photographed.

pages.text: There are many kinds of food. Where does food come from? It all comes from plants and animals. Orange juice comes from oranges. Oranges grow on orange trees. Where does orange juice come from?
pages.brief: A bright spread of many different foods fills the scene, with a glass of orange juice beside ripe oranges. Nearby, oranges hang from the branches of an orange tree, showing where the juice comes from.

pages.text: Where does milk come from? Milk comes from cows. Cows are animals. Bagels come from wheat. Wheat grows from the seeds of a wheat plant. Where do bagels come from?
pages.brief: Cows stand in a green field, with fresh milk shown nearby. A bagel rests beside stalks of tall wheat. Close by, wheat seeds and a growing wheat plant clearly show where the wheat comes from.

pages.text: Where do omelets come from? Omelets are made from eggs. Eggs come from chickens. French fries are made from potatoes. Most people think potatoes are part of the potato plant’s root. They are really part of the stem that grows below the ground. Where do French fries come from?
pages.brief: Chickens stand beside a few eggs, with an omelet shown nearby. Potatoes and golden French fries sit together. Below the ground, a potato plant’s stem is visible, clearly showing the part used for the fries.

pages.text: Where does hamburger meat come from? Hamburger meat is made from beef. Beef comes from cattle. Popcorn comes from corn. Corn is a seed from a corn plant. Where does popcorn come from?
pages.brief: Cattle graze in a green field, with hamburger meat shown nearby. Popcorn is shown beside yellow corn kernels and a tall corn plant. The corn plant and kernels clearly show where the popcorn comes from.

pages.text: Where does cheese come from? Cheese is made from milk. Milk comes from cows. The crust is made from wheat. The sauce is made from tomatoes. The cheese is made from milk. The pepperoni comes from a pig. Pizza comes from plants and animals. Where does pizza come from?
pages.brief: A whole pizza shows its crust, tomato sauce, cheese and pepperoni. Nearby stand a cow with fresh milk, tall wheat stalks, ripe tomatoes and a pig. Together they show that pizza comes from plants and animals.

books.title: A Seed Grows
books.art_why: The book shows a real plant growing, which exists in the real world today.

pages.text: A small seed falls to the ground and becomes buried in the soft soil. The seed is buried in the soft soil, and the rain falls.
pages.brief: A close-up photograph of a small seed falling onto the ground and sinking into soft soil. The seed is partly buried in the soil. Raindrops are falling from above onto the soil around the seed.

pages.text: The rain soaks into the soil that holds the small seed. 6 The small seed soaks up water from the rain.
pages.brief: A close-up photograph of soft soil in the ground holding the small seed. Rainwater has soaked into the soil around the seed. The small seed is shown taking up water from the rain-soaked soil around it.

pages.text: The water helps the seed, and roots grow down deep into the soil. The leaves and a stem grow up through the ground. The leaves gather in the sunshine.
pages.brief: A close-up photograph of the small seed in soft soil. Roots grow down deep into the soil from the seed. A stem and leaves grow up through the ground. The leaves gather in the sunshine above the soil.

pages.text: The plant uses sunshine to make food. The rain and the soil help the small plant. The plant grows taller, and more leaves grow on the stem. The roots grow longer. They go deep in the ground.
pages.brief: A photograph of the small plant growing taller in the soil. More leaves grow on the stem, and the roots grow longer deep in the ground. Sunshine falls on the leaves. The plant uses sunshine, rain and soil to make food.

pages.text: The big plant grows flowers. The flowers make seeds. A new seed falls into the soft soil. What will happen next?
pages.brief: A photograph of the big plant with flowers growing in soft soil. The flowers make seeds. A new seed falls from a flower into the soft soil below. The big plant stands in the ground with its flowers.

books.title: Whose Eggs Are These?
books.art_why: All subjects are real animals and eggs that can be photographed.

pages.text: Many animals lay eggs. Eggs can be strange and beautiful. These eggs are in a nest of twigs and soft grass. They are a beautiful sky blue. Do you know whose eggs these are? These are robin eggs.
pages.brief: A small nest made of twigs and soft grass holds a cluster of smooth, sky-blue eggs. The blue eggs rest together in the grassy cup of the nest, showing their beautiful color against the twigs.

pages.text: These tiny eggs are on the bottom of a leaf. They can be round like pearls, or they can be spiny. Whose eggs are these? They are butterfly eggs.
pages.brief: Tiny little butterfly eggs sit on the bottom of a leaf. Some eggs are round like pearls, while others are spiny. They cling to the underside of the green leaf in a small, delicate cluster.

pages.text: There are many eggs in this tiny case. It looks like light brown cotton candy, but it is made of silk. Whose eggs are these? They are spider eggs. You can find them near spider webs.
pages.brief: A tiny silk case holds many small spider eggs. The case looks like light brown cotton candy, soft and fluffy, and it hangs near spider webs. The little eggs are packed together inside the silk.

pages.text: These large eggs aren’t in a nest or case. They sit on cold rocks. But feathers help keep them warm. Whose eggs are these? These are penguin eggs. Penguins keep eggs warm with their feet and feathers.
pages.brief: On cold rocks, a penguin stands and keeps large eggs warm. The penguin holds the eggs on its feet and covers them with feathers. The big eggs are not in a nest or a case.

pages.text: This strange egg floats in the ocean. It is inside a small, tough case. Whose egg could this be? This is a shark egg.
pages.brief: A strange shark egg floats in the open ocean. The egg sits inside a small, tough case that protects it in the water. The small case drifts gently alone in the wide blue ocean water.

pages.text: These eggs float on a pond. There are tiny fish-shaped things inside each egg. Whose eggs are these? They are not fish eggs. They are frog eggs. The fish-shaped things are tadpoles.
pages.brief: Many frog eggs float on the surface of a small pond. Inside each egg, tiny fish-shaped tadpoles curl and grow. The eggs gather together on the pond surface, and the little tadpoles show clearly through.

books.title: Ants, Ants, and More Ants
books.art_why: Ants and their body parts exist in the real world and can be photographed.

pages.text: What Do Ants Look Like? Ants are insects. Their bodies have three parts, and they have six strong legs. Ants can be different colors. They can be black, brown, red, green, or yellow. Ants have two antennae that they use to touch and smell. antennae head jaws eye.
pages.brief: A close view of an ant clearly shows its three body parts, six strong legs, two antennae, head, jaws, and eye. Around it are other ants in black, brown, red, green, and yellow, with antennae raised as they touch and smell.

pages.text: Ants can be tiny or large. Some big ants are as large as a paper clip. Ants are very strong for their size. Some ants have large, strong jaws. They use their jaws to cut food and to fight.
pages.brief: Two ants are shown to compare size: a tiny ant and a big ant as large as a paper clip. A large ant uses its strong jaws to cut food. Nearby, two ants face each other with open jaws in a fight.

pages.text: Groups of Ants Most ants build nests under or on top of the ground. eggs Different ants in the nest have different jobs. The queen ant lays all the eggs.
pages.brief: A group of ants around a nest under the ground and a mound on top of the ground. The queen ant lays eggs while different ants do different jobs nearby. Eggs sit in the nest, and worker ants move around the queen and the eggs.

pages.text: Some worker ants take care of the eggs and baby ants. Some worker ants get food. Soldier ants guard the nest. Watching Ants Ants are amazing animals. You can have fun watching ants at work.
pages.brief: Ants at work around a nest. One worker ant takes care of eggs and baby ants, another worker ant gets food, and a soldier ant guards the nest. The ants are busy around the nest as they work.

books.title: Animal Eyes
books.art_why: Animal eyes and the named animals are real-world subjects that can be photographed.

pages.text: You use your eyes to see. Animals use their eyes to see, too.
pages.brief: A child’s eyes are shown looking ahead, and nearby an animal’s eyes are also shown looking ahead. The simple scene shows that people and animals both use their eyes to see the world around them.

pages.text: Animal eyes can be small or large. Some animal eyes can look very strange!
pages.brief: A group of animal eyes of different sizes is shown close together, from tiny eyes to large eyes. Some of the eyes have unusual shapes, making them look strange and inviting the viewer to compare them.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up of animal eyes fills the scene, with no clear animal body around them. The eyes are shown alone so the viewer can look closely and wonder what animal has eyes that look like this.

pages.text: This spider does. It has eight eyes that look like little dots. Most spiders can’t see very clearly. But many spiders are very good at seeing things move.
pages.brief: A spider is shown with eight eyes that look like little dots. Most spiders cannot see very clearly, but many spiders are very good at seeing things move, and the spider’s eight dot-like eyes are the focus.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up of animal eyes fills the scene, with no whole animal shown around them. The eyes are presented alone, inviting the viewer to look carefully and guess which animal has eyes that look like this.

pages.text: This owl does. Its eyes help it see well at night. An owl cannot move its eyes. It must turn its head to look around.
pages.brief: An owl is shown with eyes that help it see well at night. Because an owl cannot move its eyes, it must turn its head to look around; the owl is shown turning its head.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up of animal eyes fills the scene, with no whole animal visible around them. The eyes are shown alone, and the viewer is invited to look closely and wonder what animal has eyes that look like this.

pages.text: This kind of lizard does. Each eye can look in a different place. The left eye sees one thing. The right eye sees something different at the same time.
pages.brief: A lizard is shown with eyes that can look in different places. Its left eye sees one thing while its right eye sees something different at the same time, so each eye can point a different way.

pages.text: What animal has eyes that look like this?
pages.brief: A close-up of animal eyes fills the scene, with no whole animal shown around them. The eyes are shown alone, inviting the viewer to look closely and guess what animal has eyes that look like this.

pages.text: This dragonfly has eyes that are made up of many tiny eyes. Dragonflies are very good at seeing things move. Use your eyes to see all the animal eyes around you.
pages.brief: A dragonfly is shown with eyes made up of many tiny eyes. Dragonflies are very good at seeing things move, and the scene invites the viewer to use their own eyes to see all the animal eyes around them.
